Under the same rule `ImagePoint` keeps its internal constructor and gains no `Deconstruct`, unlike the positional `ModuleRect`: nothing in the API accepts one, so the only gain would be `var (x, y) =` over `.X` / `.Y`, and both can be added later.

### Styling stops at the finder patterns (2026-09-10)

The Playground showed a Micro QR at module size 92 % that rendered fine and decoded as nothing. The first guess, a weaker Micro QR detector, was wrong twice: Standard QR fails the same way at 92 % when no finder shape is set (the Playground hides this by defaulting to one), and 98 % already fails, so this was a cliff, not a styling trade-off.

The cause: the module shape and size were applied to the finder patterns. A data module is read by sampling its cell centre, so a gap around it costs nothing. A finder is found by scanning for the 1:1:3:1:1 run of dark and light, and a gap splits its three-module dark centre into three runs, so the ratio appears nowhere and the symbol is never located. At 24 px per module, 92 % leaves a 1.9 px sliver of white, which is enough. ZXing fails on the same renders, which settled the direction: the output was non-conformant, so the fix belonged in the writer, not the decoder.

The scope was measured. Pasting the 100 % finder back over an otherwise styled render restores every failing case (Micro QR square 92 %, Micro QR circle at 100 % and 85 %, rMQR circle 100 %, Standard QR square 92 %), so the finder is the whole defect. Alignment patterns need nothing: they are found from a predicted position by their single dark centre module, and 75 % modules still decode at versions 2 through 40. All four built-in finder shapes stay detectable with circle data modules down to 75 %, because the rings need to be continuous, not square.

Done. `WithModuleShape` styles data modules only. A `FinderPatternShape`, by default the plain square, draws the finder patterns, and `WithFinderPatternShape` moved from `QRCodeImageBuilder` to `SymbolImageBuilderBase` so every symbology has it. The Micro QR and rMQR `SymbolRenderer.Render` overloads gained the matching optional parameter, and the two matrix views now report where their finder is instead of returning `false`. The public type count is unchanged. `StyledSymbolDecodabilityTest` (28 cases at this point: three symbologies × shape × size, decorative finders, and the alignment-pattern tolerance that documents why alignment patterns are not protected) went from 18 red to green. Four rendering goldens were regenerated for the visual change, a solid finder inside otherwise styled output.

Lessons. A styling control that reaches a function pattern creates a cliff, not a trade-off, because function patterns are read as shapes and data modules as samples, so the two must not share a control. When an independent decoder rejects the output as well as ours, the bug is in the writer: adding decoder tolerance would have cost the hottest loop in decoding (finder candidates are 90 % of `FindCandidates`) to rescue symbols the library should not emit.

Benchmarks: fast path flat, styled path faster. The existing image benchmark covered only full-size squares, which this change leaves byte-identical, so two styled cases were added first. In a clean before/after with only the renderer stashed on an idle machine, `Small_512px` moved +0.8 %, `Small_2048px` +0.1 %, `Large_512px` −0.4 % and `Large_2048px` +0.6 % (all inside this class's noise, as expected for an untouched path), and the styled rows went `Large_512px_Styled` 24.36 → 23.51 ms (−3.5 %) and `Small_512px_Styled` 6.06 → 5.90 ms (−2.7 %). Allocations are identical on every row. The win comes from three rectangles per finder instead of thirty-three per-module draws.

The Playground could later expose the finder shape for Micro QR and rMQR. The default is correct without it, so this is decoration, not a fix.

### Review round on the finder rule (2026-09-10)

Three reviewer lenses ran in parallel, then three refuters checked the one claim with a design consequence. It held unanimously (3/3 not refuted), and the defect was in this change.

The finder rule had a hole on non-square canvases. Routing every styled render through a `FinderPatternShape` sent it into geometry that read one axis: `RectangleFinderPatternShape` and the two rounded variants derived `moduleSize = rect.Width / 7f` and applied it vertically too. Standard QR and Micro QR filled a canvas instead of letterboxing it, so `WithSize(900, 450)` gave cells twice as wide as tall, the light 5×5 ring came out twelve cell-heights tall inside a seven-cell box, and nothing clipped it, because the finder is drawn after the modules. Measured against the matrix at every module centre, 900×450 at 90 % modules gave 88 wrong modules, 40 of them outside the finder, against zero before the commit. The damage was not cosmetic: at 900×820 the plain render decodes and the styled one did not, while the same shrink at 900×840 decodes, so in one aspect band styling alone broke a symbol. The shapes' square assumption was pre-existing and reachable only through `WithFinderPatternShape`. Making it the default exposed it. The fix works per axis and draws ovals instead of circles in the two circle-centred shapes so they stay on the grid. On a square area every shape is byte-identical to before, as the thirteen unchanged goldens show (the seven that reach a finder shape are the ones that test it). A second pass corrected the premise for those two: they were already sized from the shorter axis, so they under-drew instead of overhanging, and the oval improves grid-following rather than fixing an overhang, as a decode at 900x540 shows, where a circle sized from the short axis fails and the oval does not.

The feature was untested for two of three symbologies. A mutant that dropped the new argument from the Micro QR and rMQR builders and reverted their crisp-edges hook passed the whole suite: the fallback is the plain square, which still decodes, so a decode assertion cannot see the difference. The new cases render with and without the requested shape and assert the bytes differ. With the SVG `crispEdges` cases the same mutant now fails eight times. The canvas extensions needed the same treatment one layer up, and the oval rewrite its own test, so the class has 59 cases.

The shipped XML docs said the feature did not exist. `MicroQRCodeImageBuilder` and `RmQRCodeImageBuilder` opened with "Icons and custom finder shapes are not offered here" on types that had just inherited `WithFinderPatternShape`. The rMQR `SymbolRenderer.Render` remark said "no icon or finder shape options" directly above its new parameter. `SKCanvasExtensions` still promised finders "follow the module shape". The canvas extensions were also broken: their Micro QR and rMQR overloads never gained the parameter, so the one entry point documented for drawing into an existing canvas could not reach the feature. Both are fixed. The round also corrected "the built-in shapes round the corners of the rings" (two of the four round nothing), the migration guide's two samples (19 bytes of content in a Micro QR that holds 13, so both threw), its escape hatch (`GetModuleRectangles` returns merged runs and cannot reproduce per-module styling, but the `[row, col]` indexer can), and the specs, Playground labels and Blazor sample that still explained the old behaviour.

The README showed the defect. Six committed sample images came from the old renderer, three of them the front page's hero images, and all six failed to decode. Regenerating `samples/ConsoleApp` fixed every one. A generated asset that documents behaviour must be regenerated when the behaviour changes, and nothing in CI says so.

One claim was refuted. A reviewer read the red count as 21, not 18, assuming the three alignment-pattern cases were green before the fix. The recorded run lists them among the failures, so the plan's number stands.

Benchmarks: unchanged. In the same two classes on an idle machine every row is inside its error bar (largest move +3.8 % on `Large_2048px`, whose bar is ±23 ms). The per-axis change adds three divisions per render.

The old finder-colour bugs did not return, but nothing guarded against them. `FinderPatternShapeColorTest` covers issues 337 (the light ring drawn dark) and 354 (a transparent background not showing through it), and was written when only Standard QR with an explicit shape could reach a `FinderPatternShape`. Styling now routes Micro QR and rMQR through one, and Standard QR reaches it unasked, so those defects apply to paths the suite never touched. All of them measured clean, opaque, translucent and transparent, with and without a gradient, but a mutant that dropped the isolated layer restoring the background under a non-opaque one passed all 8,972 tests. Nine cases were added, three symbologies x three backgrounds, and the same mutant now fails four times.

Lessons. A new default exposes geometry that was latent behind an opt-in to every caller who asks for nothing, so review the code the new default reaches, not only the code it replaces. A decode assertion cannot test a styling argument whose fallback also decodes. The test must compare against the render without it.

### `WithSize` fits instead of stretching, and padding follows the background (2026-09-10)

The `preserveAspectRatio` flag is gone, and with it the last place a supported call produced an unreadable symbol. `SymbolImageBuilderBase.PreserveAspectRatio` existed so that only rMQR letterboxed an explicit canvas while the square symbologies filled it. Its comment said they "keep the historical fill behavior", and the history shows nobody ever chose that behaviour. The initial commit's renderer (2019-01-16) computed `cellHeight = area.Height / rows` and `cellWidth = area.Width / columns` independently and was called with `SKRect.Create(0, 0, width, hight)`. Two months later `QrCode(string, Vector2Slim qrSize)` made independent width and height a public contract, `WithSize(int, int)` inherited it verbatim when the builder API landed, and #359 wrote the flag to keep rMQR out of it. The README had described the intended behaviour all along ("only need a fixed pixel box").

The stretched output could not be detected. The problem was not cosmetic. Sampled at every module centre, a stretched render is correct: the data is intact and no call throws. The finder breaks, because it is located by the 1:1:3:1:1 run along a line, and that ratio survives on one axis only. On a 33-module symbol at width 900 with the height stepped down, plain and 90 %-rectangle renders decoded to 1.67:1 and failed at 1.70:1, and circle-styled ones decoded to 1.25:1. A review round widened that sweep and the number did not hold: with a different payload of the same module count the circle-styled limit is 1.67:1, in portrait every style fails at about 1.40:1, and the two decoders disagree by direction. On wide renders this library reads far more than ZXing (354 cells against 2 in a 4,848-render sweep), and on tall ones ZXing reads far more than this library (354 against 7), only because the harness runs it with AutoRotate. The upper end of the range comes from one cell, the "https://example.com" symbol with circle modules and a circle finder in landscape, at 1.80:1. The docs now state the measured range, 1.25:1 to 1.8:1, and say no threshold is worth aiming at. `WithSize(900, 450)` returned an image no reader finds, and at 600x400 ZXing read the plain render but not the circle-styled one, while this library read both. Micro QR held to 1.64:1. Peer libraries do not allow the failure: ZXing.Net letterboxes a 900x450 request into a 315x315 symbol on an opaque white ground (measured), and CodeGlyphX, QRCoder and Net.Codecrete take a single scale or target size, so no width-and-height pair exists to get wrong.

The main decision was the pad rule, which is `clearColor ?? backgroundColor` on the builders. Letterboxing makes the pad reachable from any non-square canvas (half the image at 900x450), and the old default pad was transparent, which measurement showed is wrong to return: the same render encoded as JPEG came out with black bands (`#ff000000`), and the surface lost the opaque alpha type that lets PNG drop its alpha channel. That default already shipped on `WithModulePixelSize` + a larger `WithSize`, so one rule replaces two, at the cost of one behaviour change on a path whose geometry does not move. Naming `clearColor: SKColors.Transparent` still gives transparent surroundings. rMQR's explicit-canvas pad changes with it, from transparent to the background, which also settles its disagreement with `WithWidth`, where the 2026-08-16 review had already chosen the background for this reason.

The pad is painted around the content, not under it. Clearing the whole canvas with the pad colour and letting the renderer paint the background over the content double-blends a translucent background, so the symbol box comes out denser than the bands beside it. The clear is still right when a `clearColor` is named, because a translucent background blending over it is the documented behaviour and a test checks it. When the pad is the background there is nothing to blend, so the builder fills the up to four bands outside the content instead. Both meet the renderer on the same coordinates with antialiasing off, so the shared edges round identically and tile without a seam.

`ImageBuilderCanvasFitTest` has 68 cases after the review rounds: module centres against the fitted grid, a grid-independent check that the dark modules of a square symbology span a square, decode with and without circle styling, a ZXing cross-check at the three extreme aspects, the pad colour and opacity rules, the translucent single-coat rule, and the SVG document's two bands plus square content. 33 of them failed before the change. `FinderPatternShapeColorTest` gains thirteen cases for issues 337 and 354 on the canvas shape that only now became reachable, sampled relative to the fitted content. Seven fail against a mutant that restores the fill, ten `ImageBuilderCanvasFitTest` cases fail against one that drops the pad fill, and two against one that pads with a whole-canvas clear. Three existing tests changed: `TransparentClearWithPadding_KeepsAlpha` now asks for transparency by name (with a new sibling checking the opaque default), the rMQR padding test expects the background, and `AssertModuleCentres` samples the fitted grid, not the canvas. The full suite passes on both frameworks: 18,113 cases in Debug (17,739 passed, 374 skipped for unavailable SIMD paths) and 18,131 in Release, which enables the allocation cases Debug excludes.

The migration guide shows the pixels. Both sections of `docs/migration.md` carry a before/after pair, and the escape hatch that keeps the old padding carries a third image, all written by `samples/Dotfiles/MigrationImages_1.x-2.0.cs` into `docs/images/`. The "before" images are the real old output: the stretch comes from the low-level `SKCanvas.Render(data, 900, 450)`, which still fills the given area, and naming `clearColor` still produces the transparent pad. The generator checks each image as it writes it and prints whether it decodes, so a later change that quietly restores the fill turns the "before" image into a scanning symbol and says so on the console. Each image uses the format that shows its point: the padding pair is JPEG, where a transparent pad is flattened to black, and the `clearColor: Transparent` image is a PNG that keeps its alpha, composited over a checkerboard because a transparent pad and a white one look the same on a white page. It is a Dotfile, not a `samples/ConsoleApp` pattern, because that project shows what the current release produces, and these images show what it no longer does.

Benchmarks: unchanged, and blind to the change. Against a worktree at HEAD on an idle machine, `QRCodeImageEndToEnd` moved Small_512px 4.44 → 4.33 ms, Small_2048px 68.83 → 68.77, Large_512px 8.65 → 8.72, Large_2048px 71.20 → 69.96, Large_512px_Styled 21.92 → 22.02 and Small_512px_Styled 5.44 → 5.39. Every move is inside its error bar, and allocation is identical to the byte. A second A/B after the review rounds, base and head back to back on the same machine, resolved nothing: several rows had a BenchmarkDotNet error bar larger than their mean (Small_512px_Styled 5.79 → 6.40 ms at ±11.6, Small_2048px 74.8 → 77.3 at ±105), so it shows only that allocation is still identical to the byte on all six. The first run and the reviewer harness are the measurements that stand. A clean re-run on a quiet machine is worth doing before the release. The review round found why the class proves nothing: every case uses a square canvas, so the fitted rectangle is the canvas, `FillAround` never runs and the opacity decision never differs. Two cases that exercise it were added, `Small_NonSquare_900x450` and `Small_ModulePixelSize_InFrame`. On those shapes the change is a win: a pad that used to be transparent now makes the surface opaque, so the encoder drops the alpha channel and the unpremul pass. The review measured this on a pinned-worktree harness, not BenchmarkDotNet, at −29 % wall clock for `WithModulePixelSize(8) + WithSize(400, 400)` and −26 to −30 % for rMQR `WithSize`. No benchmark case backs the rMQR figure, because `RmQRImageEndToEnd` exercises only the `WithWidth` path, which never had a pad.

The low-level renderer stays as it was, and that is now documented. The `SymbolRenderer.Render(canvas, area, …)` and `SKCanvas.Render` overloads for the square symbologies still fill the given area, so a caller who wants pre-distorted modules (an output device whose dot pitch differs by axis is the one real use case anyone named) can still draw them. The review found that only the rMQR overload mentioned stretching, so the escape hatch looked like an oversight. Both types' XML docs now state the rule, the threshold it fails at, and why rMQR differs.

The asymmetry itself stands as F1 in the Follow-ups table above, for its own PR. Its resolution is also recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md), which survives this plan.

### Adversarial review of the canvas fit (2026-09-10)

Five lenses ran in parallel, then three refuters checked the one claim that changed code. It was a regression in this change: single-precision `matrixSize * (canvas / matrixSize)` can land just above the canvas, so the centring offset comes back about 1.5e-5 low, and flooring it loses a whole pixel. The claim held unanimously (3/3 not refuted), a fourth agent measuring performance reproduced it independently, and the SVG output shows it as `<rect fill="white" x="-1" y="-1" width="450" height="450"/>`. On a square canvas the symbol fits exactly, so that -1 opened a one-pixel band of pad along the far edges of an image that should have none, shifted the symbol up and left, and flipped `ContentCoversCanvas`, losing the opaque surface. With the default colours it is invisible, because the pad is then the background beside it. A distinct `clearColor` shows it, and 4 to 5.5 % of (version, canvas) pairs are affected. It is absent at `5b8a3a1`, because the square symbologies did not reach the letterbox path before this change.

The first fix was wrong. Clamping the offset at zero rescued the case where the true offset is zero and left every other integer offset one pixel low, so a canvas whose leftover divides evenly came out with bands 2 px apart (a 45-module symbol at 200x400 gave 99 and 101). The round-two reviewer found it by attacking the fix, not the original defect. The arithmetic needs slack, not a clamp: the offset absorbs 1e-3 before flooring, orders of magnitude above the error and below anything a viewer could see. Three test helpers had copied the pre-fix formula and were updated, or they would describe a grid the builder no longer draws on.

Every number the change published was wrong. The 1.67:1 and 1.25:1 thresholds came from one symbol, one styling and one orientation. Re-measured across three symbols (two of 33 modules, one of 45), four styles and both orientations, failures appear from about 1.25:1 and nothing survives past about 1.8:1: the styled limit is 1.67:1 with a different payload of the same module count, portrait fails at about 1.40:1 for everything, and ZXing disagrees with this library in both directions. "In our decoder and in ZXing alike" was false. The docs now state the range and say no threshold is worth aiming at, which is more useful.

Three reviewers independently found the migration guide's own escape hatch broken. `SKCanvas.Render` clears the whole canvas itself, so the guide's preceding `Clear(SKColors.White)` was dead code, and the recommended replacement produced a half-transparent image, the failure the guide's next section describes. The guide also had these errors, now corrected:

- the 2.0.0 opener and the summary table both said the release was renames and `using` lines, with three behaviour sections below them
- "`WithModulePixelSize` is unaffected" contradicted the padding section twelve lines later
- the non-square warning added to `SymbolRenderer` and `SKCanvasExtensions` sat on the type, where C# tooling never shows it, instead of on the members.

Mutation testing found what the new suite missed. Removing `Math.Floor`, dropping half of the too-small-canvas guard, and collapsing the opacity decision to the pad colour all left the single-framework suite green. Those three now have cases, as do a translucent `clearColor`, a clear colour showing through a transparent background, and the three pad bands nothing had sampled. A third round found two more: the single-coat rule was tested only on a letterbox pad, which is two bands with no corner, so a mutant widening the side bands over the corners survived. Nothing bounded the epsilon from above, so 1e-2 passed although it is past the geometric margin. That margin is now measured, and a PR review found the first measurement wrong. The bound was stated for a 159-module matrix, which the builder's own `WithQuietZone` can reach, but the generator options and the data constructors cap the quiet zone at 10,000, not 10, so a caller can build a 20,000-module matrix through ordinary public API, and a real offset can then sit as close as 2.5e-5 below a whole pixel, not 2.5e-3. An exact-integer oracle found the consequence: `RmQRCodeData(R7x139, 195)` on a 533x402 canvas has an exact offset of 1057/1058, which 1e-3 rounded up to a whole pixel. Only a rectangular matrix can do this, because a square one puts both offsets on halves. The fix computes the fit in double instead of reading it back from the renderer's float rectangle, which drops the arithmetic error to about 1e-10, five orders of magnitude under the tightest geometric bound, so an epsilon of 1e-6 separates the two at every matrix size the data types accept. The Debug suite went from 18,083 cases to 18,113.

Benchmarks: the old note was true but measured nothing. Every case in `QRCodeImageEndToEnd` uses a square canvas, so `FillAround` never ran and the opacity decision never differed. Two cases were added for the shapes that exercise it, and on those the change is a win: a pad that used to be transparent now makes the surface opaque, measured at -29 % wall clock for `WithModulePixelSize(8) + WithSize(400, 400)`.

The round produced two follow-ups, both in the Follow-ups table. F1 is the low-level renderer asymmetry. F2 came from the API lens noticing that the padding section leads readers into `WithColors` resetting colours they had already set. A survey of four other libraries found none that asks a caller to choose between override and merge, so the answer is the single-colour setters they all provide, not a semantics change to `WithColors`. Both are additive or separable, and neither blocks 2.0.0.

Lessons. A fix needs the same adversarial attention as the defect: the clamp looked right, passed the four tests written for the original symptom, and was wrong for every other value of the same variable. A measured number covers only what was measured (one symbol, one orientation), and publishing it as a threshold invites someone to design against it. State the range and the conditions, or say there is no number. "Historical" in a comment is a claim to check: this one meant a 2019 expression nobody revisited, not a decision anyone would defend, and reading the first commit settled in minutes what the comment had protected for years. A test of a call's shape says nothing about its behaviour: `WithSize_CustomSize_GeneratesCorrectSize` asserted the output was 300x400 and passed before and after a change that altered every pixel in it. The suite's silence about `WithSize(900, 450)` was itself the evidence: the one test that touched that canvas asserted module centres, not that it decodes.

### The low-level renderer fits its area (2026-09-11)

The last supported call that stretched a symbol is gone. `SymbolRenderer.Render` and the `SKCanvas.Render` extensions for Standard QR and Micro QR now draw the symbol at one uniform module scale, centred in the area, with the background over the whole area, as rMQR's overload always has. The public `GetFinderPatternRect` and `GetIconRects` fit the same way, because a caller hands them the area passed to `Render`. Everything below the fit was already per-axis (each draw routine divides the area's width and height independently), so the change computes one rectangle once and passes it where the area used to go. Only the background keeps the caller's area. Measured with this library's decoder, a 900x450 area (Standard and Micro QR) and a 200x280 portrait slot with circle modules and an icon did not decode before and now do, 512x480 decodes both ways with different pixels, and a square area is pixel-identical.

Checking the plan's order removed half of it. F1 said the builders needed an axis-aware module size first, because fitting the renderer would remove the only way to pre-distort a symbol for an output device whose dots are not square. It would not: a 2:1 canvas scale over a square area reproduces the old fill with 0 differing pixels at 900x450, 600x400, 512x480 and 300x700 for plain modules and finders in a solid colour (styled output is drawn in the square and stretched with it, so it can differ), and a square area passes through the fit unchanged, so the escape hatch never depended on the stretched area. The use case was named in the #400 review to justify keeping the fill and has no report behind it, so `WithModulePixelSize(x, y)` waits for a request (F1). For whoever builds it, the anisotropy must be a canvas transform over square cells. A non-square content rectangle no longer changes anything, because the renderer fits it to a square, and a path that skipped the fit to draw non-square cells would still get styled modules wrong: `CircleModuleShape` sizes its dot from the shorter side of the cell (with the old fill, 4x8 px of ink in an 8x8 cell after a simulated 2:1 playback, against 8x8 through the transform), and the rounded shapes take their corner radius from that side, so their corners come out uneven.

The fit is the square on the shorter side, with slack for float rounding. `GetLetterboxedArea` computes `n * (side / n)`, which in single precision need not return `side`, so the square symbologies take the centred square on the shorter side instead. The first version compared the sides exactly, which was right only at integer coordinates: `SKRect.Create(x, y, s, s)` stores right and bottom as rounded sums, so a square at fractional coordinates comes out a float step from square in over half of random cases, and shrinking it by that step moved module edges by a pixel at some offsets and made fitting depend on how often it ran. So an area whose sides differ by no more than rounding can make, two float steps at each axis's largest coordinate, comes back as given. That keeps every square render identical (the golden-pixel tests did not move) and makes fitting twice the same as fitting once, which the helpers rely on: the renderer hands them the area it already fitted, a caller hands them the original, and both get the same rectangle. The slack is measured from each axis's largest absolute coordinate, so squares near the origin, at negative coordinates where a translated canvas puts them, and far from the origin behave the same. The first slack, 1e-6 of the largest coordinate, was eight to sixteen float steps. At 1e7, where a step is a pixel, it took a 400x410 area for a square and stretched every module by 2.5 %, so the slack is now the rounding bound and no more. One step per axis is not enough: a square whose edges are each scaled, as a canvas scale gives, rounds up to about 1.1 steps per axis, measured over two million of them, so a one-step slack would shrink real squares. The two axes are scaled separately before they are added, because the sum of two coordinates near the top of the float range overflows to infinity, and an infinite slack takes any area for a square. Two steps is the floor, not a margin: across three million squares per construction, `SKRect.Create` and centre-and-half need one step per axis, and a canvas scale and `SKMatrix.MapRect` need two. A rectangle far from the origin can therefore pass as square, and this cannot be excluded: a 400x600 area at 1e9 is stored as 384x576, one and a half steps from square, closer than a real scaled square gets. A test records that limit. No symbol renders at those coordinates either. In the same round the icon's module counts moved to 64-bit arithmetic: `IconBorderModules = int.MaxValue` overflowed the total to a negative number, which passed both limits and drew a background border 2.3e10 units across. All three symbologies refuse an inverted area (a negative width or height) and a non-finite one with `ArgumentException`. The extensions check before they clear the canvas. The first cut pushed an inverted area 15,000 to 20,000 pixels outside a 400x200 area through a plain `Math.Min` of the signed sides, the second mirrored it inside, as the area taken literally had, and rMQR, untouched by either, still drew 15,077 pixels outside a vertically inverted area. Refusing it holds up: an inverted rect reads two ways, a mirror or the same bounds written backwards, and for an asymmetric symbol those are different pictures. Skia sorting an inverted rect before filling it is no guide, because a filled rect looks the same either way. The one real use behind the mirror reading, a transfer print or a sticker read through glass, is a canvas scale of -1 about the area, which all three symbologies' decoders read back. A zero-size area draws nothing instead of throwing, because a canvas before layout or a collapsed panel produces one routinely and a paint callback gains nothing from an exception. The renderer returns before drawing anything, because elements sized in pixels instead of cells survive a symbol with no size: a percent-sized icon's border drew a 4x4 square around an icon with no size, and a caption or a caller-written module shape draws whatever size it likes. The test is on the fitted symbol, not the area, so a sliver one float step wide, whose centred square rounds to no height, stops there too, and `GetIconRects` gives empty rectangles at the centre for those areas. The render still validates the icon settings at any size. Otherwise a collapsed panel would accept an icon that throws the moment the panel opens. The canvas extensions check every argument before they clear, not only the area, so a refused call leaves the canvas as it was. That also refuses `NaN` for `moduleSizePercent`, which the old `is < 0f or > 1.0f` let through into a symbol drawn without data modules, and a `GradientDirection` outside the enum, which used to clear the canvas, paint the background and only then throw from the shader call. The review round after the "every argument" claim tested it and found both. The background is still painted before the fit is tested, because the area is the caller's and only the symbol is missing: moving that draw behind the test had cost an area longer than about 2^25 to 1 its background, where the centred square's offset swallows its side. rMQR keeps `GetLetterboxedArea` as it was.

`SymbolRendererAreaFitTest` has 179 cases per framework. They decode through all three entry points (renderer, area extension, size extension) for Standard and Micro QR at 900x450, 300x900 and 600x400, with rMQR as the reference. 600x400 decoded even when stretched, so that row checks that a readable canvas stays readable, not a lost fit. A grid-free check confirms that the dark modules span a square centred in the area, with the background over the whole area and nothing outside it. Every draw path is compared pixel for pixel with the same symbol drawn into its fitted square: circle modules, gaps, a circle finder, a gradient, and a translucent background with a finder shape for the layer path, because the plain case alone let through five mutants that each drew a styled symbol stretched. The extensions are compared byte for byte, in order, with the renderer. An order-insensitive `IsEquivalentTo` on the image bytes had been blind to placement and took minutes per case. All three symbologies must refuse inverted and non-finite areas through the renderer, both helpers and the extensions (before the canvas is cleared, and a negative size on the width/height overloads), as well as finite edges further apart than a float holds, a null symbol and a `moduleSizePercent` outside 0 to 1 or `NaN`, each leaving the canvas untouched. An undefined gradient direction and a null canvas are refused the same way. An area whose symbol has no size must draw nothing through every overlay sized in pixels (a percent icon, a caption, a caller-written shape drawing a fixed dot) for a zero width, a zero height and a sliver on each axis. `GetIconRects` must give empty rectangles at the centre for the same four and still refuse an invalid icon there, by type rather than by base class. An area too long for any symbol must still paint its background, and a -1 canvas scale about the area must mirror the upright render exactly. `GetFinderPatternRect` must outline the drawn finder, and `GetIconRects` must be square and centred for module and percent sizing. `GetSquareArea` runs over 2,000 seeded fractional squares (ordinary, near the origin, negative, within 1.2e7 of it, and five with separately scaled edges that need both float steps of slack), 1,500 fractional rectangles for idempotence and helper agreement, an area near the top of the float range, and five areas more than rounding from square that must still be fitted, one a hundredth of a pixel off at a large offset and two 5 and 10 px off at 1e7, so a tolerance loosened or tightened either way is caught. 28 of the first 40 cases failed before the change. The other 139 were added for the defects and surviving mutants found after it, for refusing inverted, overflowing and otherwise invalid arguments, and for the symbol with no size. The sliver exists on both axes because the first one collapsed only the height, and a guard testing only the width survived every test in the class. Each of three review rounds found a gap the previous round left:

- a positive case for `GradientDirection.None`, which the new argument check could have refused unnoticed
- the order in which the size overloads report a null canvas, symbol and size
- a control proving the empty-area cases land on the bitmap at all, without which eight of them passed by drawing off it
- measuring the fit instead of assuming it in the too-long-area case, whose rMQR row had asserted a state rMQR does not reach until three powers of two later.

In `StyledSymbolDecodabilityTest`, `DecorativeFinder_NonSquareRect_RingsFollowTheGrid` draws each finder shape straight into a non-square rect, the only remaining path that produces one, and three comments that still described builder canvases as non-square now say what they test. The full suite passes on both frameworks, 18,509 cases in Debug (18,135 passed, 374 skipped for unavailable SIMD paths).

The docs state what was measured, and the migration images check it. The generator made its stretched "before" image through the fill. It now asks for the stretch with a canvas scale over a square area, which gives the old fill's pixels exactly for plain modules in a solid colour, and regenerating left the existing images byte-identical. The guide's renderer section shows the renderer's own use instead of repeating the 900x450 banner: a 200x300 slot on a 280x380 card, stretched before (this library's decoder misses it, but ZXing.Net and zxing-cpp read it) and fitted after (all three read it). The captions said no reader finds the stretched images, which zxing-cpp contradicts for both, so each caption now names the readers and the generator checks all three against it. Around the change, the `clearColor` docs on the extensions now say the background covers the area and the clear colour shows inside it only through a translucent background, `IconData`'s percent sizing is a percentage of the symbol's side, the per-symbology spec pages link to the measurements in `qrcode-symbologies.md` instead of restating them, and the Playground's API page is regenerated.

Benchmarks: allocation identical, time inside the noise. `QRCodeImageEndToEnd` and `MicroQRImageEndToEnd` ran back to back against a worktree at `main` after the final change (ShortRun). Allocation is identical to the byte on all twelve cases, and the largest mean increase is +7.8 % on `M4_ImageDecode_Span`, a decode case the change does not touch (Small_512px 4.59 → 4.79 ms, Small_NonSquare_900x450 7.16 → 7.51, Large_512px 9.43 → 9.22, M4_512px 5.12 → 4.59). An earlier run had one row past +10 %, M4_128px at 323 → 373 us with a ±424 us error bar. Re-measured alone with base and head alternating, it came to +8.8 % and then +2 %. The fit adds a few float operations per render and nothing in the per-module loops. ShortRun on this machine cannot resolve a few percent either way.

Lessons. An escape hatch recorded in review needs the check a defect gets: this one was written down as the only route, and one canvas transform showed it was not needed, which turned a two-part PR with a new public API into a fit and the two helpers that follow it. A claim about pixels or readers covers every case it does not exclude: "bit for bit" had been tested only at integer coordinates, "no reader finds it" only with this library's decoder, and "pixel for pixel" only with plain modules, and each broke on the first case outside what was measured. Listing exceptions one at a time kept missing new ones (circle finders, diagonal gradients, caption icons). Stating what is exact and calling the rest different held. A number restated on a second page drifts from the first: the Micro QR spec map had picked up a reader that cannot read Micro QR, so it now links to the one place the measurements live.

### Phase 3b, option nullability and colour setters (2026-09-12)

Done. The builders' colour options are values again: `WithColors(SKColor codeColor, SKColor backgroundColor)` with both arguments required, plus `WithCodeColor`, `WithBackgroundColor` and `WithClearColor`. `WithModuleShape` and `WithFinderPatternShape` no longer take `null`: both throw `ArgumentNullException`, and a caller passes `RectangleModuleShape.Default` / `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` for plain squares. The fields behind the colours and the module shape hold `SKColors.Black`, `SKColors.White` and `RectangleModuleShape.Default` instead of `null`, so the four `?? default` resolutions inside the builder are gone. `WithGradient(null)`, `WithIcon(null)` and `WithClearColor(null)` are unchanged, and their XML docs now say the `null` means an absent option, not a default value. The static `SymbolRenderer` and `SKCanvas.Render` surfaces keep every `null` they had, for the language reason recorded above. The new `SymbolImageBuilderColorOptionTest` (11 cases) guards it. The old `WithColors_NullColors_ReturnsBuilder` became `WithClearColor_NullClearColor_ReturnsBuilder`, the part of it that still exists. 78 call lines were rewritten across 20 files in tests, samples, the Playground and the BlazorWasm sample, and both approved API listings were regenerated (the core listing is unchanged, and the renderer's gains three members and changes three signatures). The full suite passes: 18,531 tests, 0 failures, both target frameworks.

Rendering, not reading the code, decided the finder shape row. It entered this phase as "keep the null, fix the doc", because omitting the shape and passing `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` take different paths: when omitted, the finders are drawn with the modules, and the square is substituted only once the modules are styled. Comparing the bitmaps settled it: 0 differing bytes of 360,000 with plain modules, on an opaque and on a transparent background. Two paths give one raster output, so the null was a second spelling of a named value like the others, and the parameter joined them. The circle-modules case should not have been cited with those: styling substitutes the square for both spellings, so it compares one path with itself and is a boundary case, not evidence. What the measurement also missed is recorded below. The path survives as an implementation detail (a builder never asked for a finder shape still merges the finders into the module runs), and the Playground and BlazorWasm samples keep their "Auto" option by not calling the setter, which is the same state stated explicitly.

The golden-pixel tests show that nothing renders differently. They were expected to pass without regeneration, because the renderer resolved `null` to the values the builder now holds (`?? SKColors.Black`, `?? SKColors.White`, `?? RectangleModuleShape.Default`), so only what a caller can express changes. A new test checks this directly by rendering `WithModuleShape(RectangleModuleShape.Default)` against a builder that never called it and comparing the bitmaps byte for byte. The sample gallery agrees at a larger scale: `samples/ConsoleApp` regenerated here and in a worktree at `main` gives byte-identical output for every file it writes. Four of those files differ from what is committed, on `main` as well as here, so that drift predates this phase and was left out of this change.

The Playground was verified by hand because `QrInterop` changed. A published Debug WASM build encoded through the paths this phase touches, Standard QR, Micro QR (M2, 17x17) and rMQR (512x95, so the rectangular geometry is real and not a stale preview), each with plain and circle modules and with the finder shape both on Auto and set to the square explicitly. Every one rendered and passed the page's own self-decode, with no console errors. The main case to check was Auto, which is now "do not call the setter" instead of "pass null".

Benchmarks: allocation identical, time inside the noise. For `QRCodeImageEndToEnd` against a worktree at `main` (ShortRun, net10.0), allocation matches on all eight cases to the hundredth of a kilobyte, and every mean moved between +0.1 % and -7.8 %, against ShortRun errors of ±2 to ±8 ms on the larger cases. Nothing should have moved (the builder resolves two fewer `??` per render, outside any per-module loop), and the numbers agree. The first baseline run was discarded: it ran while this session was building and testing, and it made `main` look 40 % slower than it is. A benchmark that shares the machine measures the machine.

Lessons. A null that resolves to a named constant on arrival is a second spelling: the API pays for it while the implementation discards it in one line, and `var shape = moduleShape ?? RectangleModuleShape.Default;` was the whole case for removing it. The Playground showed the symptom long before anyone read it as one: `_ => null, // rectangle (default)` needed a comment to say what `RectangleModuleShape.Default` says by itself. A different code path is not a different state, and only the output tells which it is. That moved the finder shape from "keep the null" to "remove it" after the table was written. Two more lessons concern telling cases apart. The mechanical sweep again reached `samples/Dotfiles/FinderPatternAlwaysBlack.cs`, the file pinned to the released `SkiaSharp.QrCode@1.0.0` whose header says to skip it, the same finding as the Phase 2 sweep, so any sweep needs a second grep of `samples/Dotfiles`. An assertion about a transparent pixel must compare alpha, not colour: `SKColors.Transparent` carries white channels, a rendered transparent pixel carries zeroed ones, and the first version of the padding test failed on `Red 255 vs 0` while the code was correct.

### Adversarial review of Phase 3b (2026-09-12)

Five reviewers and twelve refutation agents left four findings. The API change itself was sound: an 864-configuration parity matrix against a worktree at `main` (3 symbologies × 4 backgrounds × 3 clear colours × 4 sizings × 3 module shapes × PNG and SVG) gave 864 identical hashes, and each removed `??` resolution was confirmed dead. The round found a claim wider than its measurement, a spec sentence that justified more than it could, a migration guide that promised the compiler would catch what it cannot, and four regressions the new tests would have missed.

The equivalence claim was true for raster and false for SVG. "Omitting `WithFinderPatternShape` and naming `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` render identically" was measured on PNG at one canvas size on an opaque background, and stated without qualification in the migration guide, the XML docs and the spec. Three verifiers independently reproduced one counterexample: with a background alpha below 255, naming the shape moves the finders onto a pass that cuts their light rings out with `SKBlendMode.Clear` inside a `SaveLayer`, `SKSvgCanvas` drops the layer, and the emitted document contains no finder patterns. This library's own decoder reads the omitted-spelling SVG and fails on the named one, six cases out of six. The defect predates the phase and reaches any styled symbol, because styling substitutes a square finder. The phase added an instruction that led callers into it. The claim is now stated per output kind, the spec records the limitation, the migration guide leads with "replace a `null` by not calling the setter", and the README and the renderer's own XML docs carry the warning. The fix belongs to the renderer and gets its own change: a ring drawn as geometry instead of an erase survives both canvas kinds.

A measurement that compares a thing with itself proves nothing. The third case cited as evidence, circle modules at 0.85, passes `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` in both spellings, because `ResolveFinderShape` substitutes it for any styled module set, so only one path ran. Its test (`WithFinderPatternShape_RectangleDefault_MatchesTheOmittedShape(styledModules: true)`) is a tautology and stays only as a boundary case.

The rule's exemption for the static surface was broader than the language justifies. "A C# optional parameter needs a constant default" holds for the shapes and for every parameter of the `SKCanvas.Render` extensions, but not for `SymbolRenderer.Render`'s `codeColor` and `backgroundColor`, which are required parameters typed `SKColor?` on all three overloads: consistency with the extensions keeps them nullable, not the language. Their XML docs said "Black when omitted" of a parameter that cannot be omitted, and the plan claimed those docs were corrected when the commit had not touched the file. The docs are now corrected. The signatures are a separate decision (taken 2026-09-13, below).

"Compile-time break, no behaviour change" was false for the audience the guide names. With nullable reference types off (every C# 7.3 consumer, which the guide addresses in its own section), `WithModuleShape(null, 0.9f)` and `WithFinderPatternShape(null)` compile with no diagnostic and now throw `ArgumentNullException` where they used to render plain squares. A netstandard2.0 / C# 7.3 consumer build confirmed it: `0 Warning(s), 0 Error(s)`, then a throw at the setter. The guide now says so and tells the reader to search by hand. Its `is not null` snippet, which does not compile at C# 7.3, became `!= null`.

Four mutations survived the suite and now fail it. Mutation testing found that `WithClearColor` could reset the code colour, `WithModuleShape` could drop a finder shape set before it, `WithClearColor(null)` could stop un-setting, and `UseCrispEdges` could lose its `_moduleSizePercent == 1.0f` conjunct, all with no test failing. Not every gap was a missing call sequence: two are sampling gaps, where tests already exercised the path but asserted something shape-agnostic or default-coloured. A second sweep found the mirror direction open too (a colour setter could wipe the clear colour or all three shape options, and an explicitly named square finder could fall back to the module pass), because every new test set the victim option first. Nine test methods were added, six to `SymbolImageBuilderColorOptionTest` and three to `QRCodeImageBuilderSvgTest`, each confirmed red under its mutation and green without it. crispEdges on gapped squares is a real defect, not a cosmetic one: rasterized at a non-integer scale, the quantized gaps vary by 50 % across the symbol.

The full suite passes: 18,569 tests in Release, 0 failures, both target frameworks (18,551 in Debug, where the allocation assertions do not run). The committed API page (`src/FeatherQR.Playground/wwwroot/api/index.html`) was regenerated, which the phase had missed and both neighbouring pull requests did. The approved listing is unchanged, because the round touched only documentation and tests.

Items left for their own changes are filed as rows, not prose: the SVG finder-erase defect is F3, `SymbolRenderer.Render`'s two required `SKColor?` parameters are F4, the surviving optional-argument resets on `WithModuleShape` and `WithFormat` are F5, the untested interactions between the layout setters and everything else are F6, and the NaN hole in the size-percent guard is F7. One more was small enough to fix here. `SegmentDecoderStatusOrderTest` built a reflectance-reversed symbol as bait for the retry it says must not happen, and passed whether or not that symbol was drawn at all, because a bait that collapses to black-on-black satisfies "the normal symbol's result wins" as a correct one does. Both polarity tests now first decode the reversed symbol alone and assert it reads the single character that would have fitted the short destination, the premise the rest of the test rests on. As with the other gaps, a mutant proved it: with `WithColors` ignoring its code colour, the class passed 24 of 24 before and fails the two polarity tests after. Deferred work goes in the Follow-ups table, because a Progress log entry records what happened and nobody searches it for what is left.

Each of four review rounds found the previous round's fix over-claiming. Round 1 corrected "renders identically" to "identical in raster". Round 2 showed even that was too strong (a gradient over a non-opaque background differs by a few least-significant bits), and that "leave the setter uncalled" is no workaround when the modules are styled, because styling substitutes the shape anyway. Round 3 found that the remedy example in the migration guide had no padding, so its `WithClearColor(SKColors.Transparent)` painted nothing, and the sentence beside it promised a transparent quiet zone, which is part of the background fill and never transparent. Round 4 found that round 3's provenance sentence was wrong in the other direction (Micro QR and rMQR reach the defect through styled modules too, with no setter call), that the generated API page had been regenerated before the last XML doc edit and so shipped the refuted workaround, and that the README carried the same no-padding example the guide had just corrected. Each was written after a real measurement taken on a different configuration than the one the prose showed. Hence the rule, and the reason this entry names its configurations: a claim is only as wide as the configuration it was measured on, and an example in prose is a configuration of its own. The round-4 probes reran the exact snippets from the guide and the README, not their shape.

The same rule caught tests. Round 3 found that TUnit's `IsEquivalentTo` ignores order, so six bitmap comparisons would have accepted a rotated image. They now use an explicit `SequenceEqual` helper. Round 4 found that widening an SVG query from `rect` to every element had no effect, because the geometry helper reads only `x`/`y`/`width`/`height`, so the widening was reverted instead of kept with a comment describing something the code does not do.

### The finder ring is a hole (2026-09-13)

Done. This is F3, which proved to be 2.0.0 work, not a follow-up, because the fix removes public API. A `FinderPatternShape` now draws only the dark modules, so the light ring is whatever the renderer already put beneath the finder. This round drew the square as five rectangles (four bands around the 5×5 hole, then the centre) and each of the three curved shapes as one even-odd `SKPath`. The review round below replaced two of those three, because a path costs 45 KB of SVG that an oval does not, so read the geometry there. The `SaveLayer` / `SKBlendMode.Clear` pass that erased the ring on non-opaque backgrounds is gone from both the Standard QR path and `DrawSingleFinder`, and with it the two `Draw` overloads that carried a light colour or paint, because a shape that paints its ring can be right on a translucent background only by erasing. The finder's antialiasing now follows the finder shape, not the module shape. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` lost exactly the ten overload lines. The README warning, the migration guide's "known limitation" section (now "Finder shapes draw the dark modules only", with the custom-shape migration), the spec paragraph and the six XML doc sentences were rewritten together, as the test documenting the limitation said they should be. The full suite passes on both target frameworks, 18,587 tests.

Before the fix, on browser-rasterised SVG, this library's decoder failed all four non-opaque Standard QR cases at 512x512 (alpha 254 and 128 named, alpha 128 and 0 styled) and read the two opaque ones. The F3 row's "6 of 6" counted a wider sweep across the three symbologies, so quote the configuration in question. The translucent document had 9 fewer `rect`s on Standard QR and 3 fewer on Micro QR and rMQR, the whole finder including its dark outer square. After the fix, the translucent document equals the opaque one once `fill-opacity` is stripped, on all three symbologies and all four built-in shapes (`DecorativeFinder_TranslucentBackground_DrawsTheSameSvgElements`, 12 cases). In raster, the named square and the omitted setter are now 0 pixels apart under a gradient over an alpha-128 background at 300, 512, 513, 777 and 900 px, where the layer used to cost one step of one channel. The spec sentence that recorded that exception is now in the past tense. Three approval goldens changed, the curved-finder ones, and the round below moved two of them again. Measured against `main` at the end, they differ by 164, 128 and 122 pixels of 13,456, every one inside a finder box (checked, 0 outside) and on a ring edge, max delta 57, because a hole edge is rasterised once where a light oval over a dark one was rasterised twice. The square-finder goldens, `standardqr-circle-modules` included, did not move.

Benchmark delta: `QRCodeImageEndToEnd`, whose two styled cases reach the substituted square finder, ran back to back against `main` at the end of the review rounds. `Large_512px_Styled` went 23.95 → 24.07 ms and `Small_512px_Styled` 5.99 → 5.76 ms, both far inside a run-to-run error of ±1.0 ms and ±0.27 ms on that pass, and the plain cases moved by the same fraction in both directions, which is the machine, not the change. Allocation, the deterministic half, went down: 204.71 → 203.91 KB and 28.18 → 27.77 KB. The two rounded shapes allocate one `SKPathBuilder` and one `SKPath` per finder, which no benchmark case covers. The circle and the square allocate neither, because a stroked oval and five rectangles need no path.

Lessons. The layer compensated for a contract, not a canvas: "paint the ring light" is wrong on every background that is not the light colour, and erasing made it right only where erasing exists. Drawing the ring as nothing needs no compensation anywhere. For a defect in one backend, ask whether the drawing expresses something the other backend also had to fake. A test that documents a limitation should say what replaces it: the old `LosesTheFinderPatterns` test named the named-shape arm as the one thing to keep, and that arm survived.

### Adversarial review of the finder-ring fix (2026-09-13)

Five reviewers raised twelve claims, and three independent verifiers each upheld all twelve. The drawing itself had no defect: geometry, even-odd nesting, `fill-rule` emission, paint state and 540 styled decode configurations were checked against the old renderer and came back identical or better. The findings were in the compiler, the tests and the prose around it.

Done. `SKPath.AddOval` / `AddRoundRect` are `[Obsolete]` in SkiaSharp 4.148 ("use `SKPathBuilder`"), and the fix had introduced 36 CS0618 warnings, 9 sites across 4 target frameworks. A clean rebuild is silent again with `SKPathBuilder` plus `Detach()`, which replaces the whole mutable `SKPath` construction API. `FinderPatternShape.RequiresAntialiasing` is now `abstract`, as `ModuleShape`'s already was: the renderer assigns it instead of OR-ing it, so the inherited `false` had silently become "draw my curves aliased" for any custom shape that did not override it (on Standard QR beside `CircleModuleShape`, a custom curved finder without the override lost 1,063 antialiased pixels at 232 px and 2,267 at 464). Four XML doc passages on `SymbolImageBuilderBase` (`WithModuleShape`, `WithFinderPatternShape` and its `finderPatternShape` param, `SaveToSvg`) still told callers the defect was live and to give SVG an opaque background. That file was not in the fix's diff, and its text ships in IntelliSense and in the generated API page. `docs/migration.md` claimed the two spellings of a square finder are "element-identical in SVG, on any background", which is false and always will be (30 elements apart on Standard QR at every alpha: five rectangles per finder against fifteen merged runs). The spec said the same in the past tense. The README kept a dangling "with one exception noted below" pointing at the warning the fix deleted. The migration guide's custom-shape sample used `rect.Width / 7f` for both axes, which no built-in does (32.7 % of the pixels differ on a 140x280 rect). It now shows the per-axis form, `SKPathBuilder`, the `RequiresAntialiasing` override and a line saying why a solid square is unscannable.

Five mutants made two new tests necessary, because the suite could not see the defect it had just fixed. With a thread-static flag that suppressed drawing in SVG output only, all of these passed: `DrawSingleFinder` drawing nothing (Micro QR and rMQR lose every finder), the three curved shapes skipping `DrawPath`, and the square shape dropping its four outer bands and keeping the 3x3 centre. `ResolveFinderShape` ignoring an explicitly named square also passed, which falsified the comment in the regression test claiming that test would catch it. Reverting the antialiasing assignment passed too, although it changes real output. The suite's two SVG assertions were an existence check on the finder's centre and an alpha-255-versus-alpha-128 invariance check, and a document that lost its finder at both alphas satisfies the second as well as a correct one. `DecorativeFinder_SvgCarriesTheWholeFinderPattern` (3 symbologies x 5 routes x 3 alphas) probes the centre and all four outer edges of every finder box, plus the four light ring midpoints, which must stay undrawn. It reads the region an element paints, so a rectangle, a path and a stroked oval answer the same query, and it asserts five elements per box for the square, which tells an explicitly named square from the fifteen merged module runs that draw the same picture. `StyledModules_FinderAntialiasing_FollowsTheFinderShape` checks the antialiasing rule in both directions on all three symbologies. (Both grew in the review round below. This paragraph describes their final form.) The five mutants now fail 8, 9, 3, 3 and 3 cases.

A second round addressed the fix's own regressions. The performance reviewer measured the even-odd path's SVG cost, and it was large: `SKSvgCanvas` writes a rectangle or an oval as one element but flattens a path into thousands of quadratic segments, so a circle finder's document went from 5.8 KB to 49.9 KB and about 5x slower to write, and the rounded-circle one from 35.7 KB to 50.4 KB, entirely because its 3x3 centre oval had been folded into the path (512x512, "https://githu" at ECC M, 29 modules). The figures move with the module count, hence the named configuration. Three verifiers reproduced both, and two independently found the fix. The ring is now expressed as whatever the SVG writer can name:

- four bands and a centre rectangle for the square
- for the circle, a one-module stroke of the middle oval, exactly the region between the 5x5 and 7x7 ovals because a circle's offset curve is another circle, plus a filled centre oval
- an even-odd path for the two rounded shapes, whose ring radii differ per contour, with any oval centre kept out of it.

In the same configuration the documents are now 5.8 KB and 35.7 KB, within a tenth of a kilobyte of what 1.x wrote (5.8 and 35.7), and decode at every alpha on all three symbologies. The raster differences against the path form are antialiasing on the ring edges with no pixel changing side (two goldens regenerated, 74 and 54 pixels of 13,456). The stroke is exact only where the cells are square, because one stroke width cannot be one module on both axes (a verifier showed the naive version painting 537 pixels outside its own box on a 20x10 grid), so a non-square rect keeps the path, and the renderer never passes one. `FinderPatternShape`'s `paint` contract changed with it: restore any property you change, instead of changing nothing.

A round-2 reviewer also showed the new SVG test was weak where it mattered. It located elements by bounding box, and a curved shape's single path has the bounding box of the whole finder, so a `CircleFinderPatternShape` mutated to draw one solid disc (no ring, unscannable) passed all twelve of its cases. It now reads real geometry: `SKPath.ParseSvgPathData` for paths, a constructed oval for `<ellipse>`, `GetFillPath` to expand a stroked outline into the band it paints, then `Contains`. The four light-ring probes now run for every shape instead of only the square, and the solid disc fails. Nine mutations were run against the finished pair, four of them aimed at the new stroke code (drop the centre, double the stroke width, skip the paint restore), and all nine fail, 3 to 10 cases each. A later sweep on the same pair found two uncovered cells, now cases of their own: the styled-module route on Micro QR and rMQR (the ordinary way in, with no finder-shape call, where an SVG-only mutation could still drop the finder), and the antialiasing rule in the other direction, where `DrawSingleFinder` could answer a constant `false` instead of the shape and no curved finder was asserted to be smooth.

The same round found two more. The approved-API gate could not see this release's own break. `tools/check_public_api.cs` printed `abstract` / `virtual` / `override` for methods but only `static` for properties, so `RequiresAntialiasing` turning abstract left `PublicAPI.approved.txt` byte-identical and the check reported "unchanged", on the one file the spec says holds the exported surface, for a change that stops an already-compiled subclass from loading. Both accessors now read the same helper. The listings gained 9 lines, all `RequiresAntialiasing` (two `abstract`, seven `override`), and the core assembly's listing did not move, so nothing else in either surface was a virtual property. The square finder also seamed under an antialiased paint: four abutting bands replaced one rectangle, and antialiased shared edges do not composite back to opaque, so a 22 %-grey line ran across the ring at both band junctions (826 intermediate pixels against 0). The renderer never passes this shape an antialiased paint, but `Draw` is public, and a custom shape that declares antialiasing and delegates to it gets one, which a verifier reproduced end to end. The shape holds the paint to the straight edges it declares and restores the flag, so the seam is gone whoever calls it, and the new `DecorativeFinder_DrawnWithAnAntialiasedPaint_RestoresItAndDrawsNoSeam` checks both that and the paint-restore contract for all four shapes.

The squareness test that chooses between the two circle formulations used `float.Epsilon`, which is not the machine epsilon but the smallest denormal, about 1.4e-45, so the comparison meant exact equality. The fit leaves two of a Standard QR's three finder rects a few ulps off square at most canvas sizes, so at 513x513, 500x512 and 900x450 two finders of three fell back to the path and the document came out at 26 KB instead of 5.9 KB, while 512x512, the size everything had been measured at, was perfect. A relative 1e-4 fixed it, and `DecorativeCircleFinder_ReachesSvgAsOvals` checks the encoding at those sizes: reverting the tolerance fails three of its four cases.

Lessons. An invariance assertion is not an existence assertion. Comparing translucent output with opaque output is satisfied by "both are empty", the failure the comparison was written to prevent, so every invariance test needs a positive claim behind it. A golden built with `WithModulePixelSize` cannot see an antialiasing change on a straight edge, because whole-pixel module edges make the flag a no-op there. All 13 approval cases have that shape, and all 13 missed the square finder losing its inherited antialiasing, so the styled raster output of every `WithSize` caller moved (around 1 % of a 512x512 circle-module render) with nothing failing, and the first migration note under-described it. The narrow reading is the true one: with antialiasing forced off for a curved finder, 3 of those 13 goldens fail, so a whole-pixel grid hides the edge kind, not the setting. A property whose default was only a hint becomes a trap once the renderer obeys it in both directions: `virtual => false` was fine while it could only turn antialiasing on. The review also found the over-claim class the Phase 3b rounds did, one release later: "element-identical" was written from a raster measurement. The last two rounds found only that class, three times over: every remaining finding was a number or description true of the previous round's code and left behind by the next (the spec's SVG sizes, this entry's own copies of them, the F3 row still saying "one even-odd path each" after the circle stopped being one, and an upper bound of 1.6 % where the measurement now tops out at 1.22 %). Prose about a measurement ages as fast as the code it measured, so a round that changes the drawing must re-run every number the previous round wrote down, not only the ones it thinks it touched.

### The renderer's colours are values (2026-09-13)

Done. `SymbolRenderer.Render`'s `codeColor` and `backgroundColor` are `SKColor` on all three overloads (F4), and the two `?? SKColors.Black` / `?? SKColors.White` resolutions moved out of the renderer into the three `SKCanvas.Render` area extensions, next to the existing `clearColor ?? SKColors.Transparent`. The size extensions delegate to the area ones, so the forward exists once per symbology. A `null` in either position is CS1503, which found the six call sites: two in one rMQR test, one Micro QR test, and the gradient samples in ConsoleApp (two) and ConsoleAppNativeAOT (one), where `codeColor: null, // Use gradient instead` was this plan's own "a comment carries what the argument cannot say" and is now `SKColors.Black`. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` changed by exactly the three `Render` lines. The rMQR spec's signature block and the nullability paragraph in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md) follow, and the migration guide has its own section. Pixels are unchanged, because the renderer already resolved the two nulls to these two colours.

`SymbolRendererColorParameterTest` had 12 cases at this point, covering three symbologies through the area extensions and the renderer and comparing bitmaps byte for byte. The forward is checked twice: omitted colours draw what black on white draws, and named colours (navy on yellow) arrive as named, with a control against black on white so a forward that ignored its arguments would fail instead of passing vacuously. The two facts a caller who must now write a code colour needs are checked the same way: under a gradient the colour is not used (black and red byte-identical, with a control against the solid render proving the gradient was drawn), and under `GradientDirection.None` it is the colour painted (byte-identical to no gradient, with a control against another colour). All 12 pass before and after the change: only what a caller can write changed, so the approved listing and the compiler give the red, and the pixel tests confirm the resolution moved without changing. The full suite passes on both frameworks, 0 failures, 374 skipped for unavailable SIMD paths.

The decision was measured before it was made. Two shapes were considered. A: the parameters become `SKColor`. C: a colourless overload beside each of the three, defaulting to black on white, so the common call shrinks to `Render(canvas, area, data)`. C was compiled against stand-in types before being judged. Every positional and named spelling binds unambiguously except `default, default` (CS0121). A mixed `(null, White)` or `(Black, null)` is CS1503. On the Standard QR overload the old `Render(canvas, area, data, null, null)` compiles, binding the two nulls to `iconData` and `moduleShape`, with pixel-identical output and no diagnostic. That is the migration the guide promises the compiler will flag, so C could not keep that promise there. It affects one overload of three, not all of them as this entry first claimed: Micro QR and rMQR have no `IconData?`, so the second `null` would have to land on `float moduleSizePercent`, and both are CS1503 (reported against the coloured candidate's `SKColor`, because the colourless one is silently inapplicable). That still did not decide it. Weighed as user experience from eight seats (first-time caller, reader of the call, SkiaSharp user, consistency with the builders and extensions, migrator, gradient user, maintainer, and the public API growth rule), C won two rows narrowly (the call reads as uniformly optional, and a gradient user on a white background writes no dead colour) and A won the rest, three outright. The `SKCanvas` a caller holds never assumes a colour, because every Skia draw call takes its paint, so a renderer that names its colours fits Skia's idiom and one that assumes them does not. Omission already exists in both the builders and the extensions, so C was a third layer offering the same default. A second signature per symbology is one more to keep in step for every later option, with the optional-parameter-plus-overload resolution hazards the `default, default` case showed. The README already taught A's spelling.

The dead argument under a gradient was examined separately and left, with reasons filed. Making the code colour a required value made visible that a gradient caller writes one that never reaches a pixel, because `darkPaint.Shader = gradientShader` replaces it. Five responses were considered:

- document it in Skia's terms, since it is `SKPaint`'s own model of a shader over a colour (chosen, and the `gradientOptions` documentation on all nine entry points now says a gradient takes precedence over the code colour and that `GradientDirection.None` paints in it)
- one overload per paint kind, the doubling A had just declined, which lets `(null, White)` compile into an `ArgumentNullException`
- a fill type replacing both parameters, the correct model but a redesign of the builders too, filed as F8
- giving the colour Skia's meaning under a shader, alpha scaling the gradient, which nobody asked for and leaves the RGB unused
- pointing gradient callers at the extensions, which clear the canvas and so are not the same call.

Lessons. An overload pair looks free until it is compiled: two nulls binding to the next two reference-typed optionals with identical pixels is the silent rebinding that overloads plus optional parameters produce, and review misses it because nothing visible changes. A dead argument that is the host API's own model is documented in that model's words, not designed around. A change to what a caller can write has no failing behaviour test to start from. The approved listing and the build give the red, and the behaviour tests show the change moved nothing.

Benchmark delta: not measured. Two `??` on a render's entry path moved from the renderer to the extensions, and nothing on a hot path changed shape.

### Adversarial review of the renderer's colours (2026-09-13)

Over five rounds the change's own logic passed the first round clean, and the writing around it did not. The first round had five reviewers, and three of its findings survived three independent refutation attempts each. The signatures, the resolution's new home, the seven former `bgColor`/`fgColor` sites, the validation order, the approved listing and the build across four target frameworks were checked then and were right. None of the four later rounds touched them. The rounds found a spelling the change left out of the migration guide, a hole it left in the tests, a generated file it did not regenerate, an overstated sentence about the option it declined, and a run of smaller inaccuracies in its own new prose. Rounds two to five each found at least one of those in the previous round's writing, including earlier versions of this paragraph: the code was right the first time, and the writing about it took five passes.

The compiler does not flag the `default` spelling, and the guide said it would. `Render(canvas, area, data, default, default)` compiled before and compiles now, with a different meaning each time: `default(SKColor?)` was `null`, which the renderer resolved to black on white, while `default(SKColor)` is transparent. Two verifiers compiled byte-identical source against a `HEAD~1` build and a `HEAD` build and measured 24,310 black plus 65,690 white pixels and a successful decode against 90,000 transparent pixels and a failed one, with zero diagnostics at `TreatWarningsAsErrors` and `AnalysisLevel=latest-all`, and the same for one `default` beside one named colour. The guide's headline, "the compiler finds every site", was false for exactly one spelling, twelve lines above a paragraph that already stated the fact it needed (`default(SKColor)` is transparent) about the extensions. Nobody in this repository or its history wrote it, and the old XML doc asked for `null`, so the impact is small. The section now says so, in the form the guide already uses for the shape setters. `Render_TransparentColors_AreDrawnAsGiven` checks the contract underneath: two transparent colours leave the canvas untouched, because nothing is substituted for them any more.

No test covered the size overloads' colour forwarding, on all three symbologies. Mutation testing found it: hardcoding black and white in the rMQR size overload's forward left the full suite green (9,325 tests on one framework, 0 failed), and so did hardcoding only the code colour in the Standard QR and Micro QR ones. The hole needed two causes. `SymbolRendererAreaFitTest`'s `NonSquareAreas()` paired rMQR with the renderer alone, so the `("rmqr", "extensionSize")` arm of its `Draw` helper was unreachable. The delegation test covering the other two size overloads passes `SKColors.Black` as the code colour, so only the background ever discriminated. `CanvasExtension_SizeOverload_ForwardsBothColors` closes it with navy on yellow through all three, compared byte for byte with the area overload over the same rectangle, plus a control against black on white so the comparison cannot go vacuous. All three fail under the mutants that used to survive, and for the rMQR ones they are the only failure in the suite. The new class's own comment, claiming the forward "is tested once" because the size overloads delegate, was the defect in small: a true statement about the production code serving as a coverage guarantee.

The next round, on the fix, found the hole only half closed. The colour arguments were now tested, but the rest of what the rMQR size overload forwards was not, because the `("rmqr", "extensionSize")` arm was still unreachable. Transposing that overload's width and height (`SKRect.Create(0, 0, height, width)`) passed all 9,331 tests on that framework, the same suite plus this round's six new cases, while the same mutation on the Standard QR overload failed four. The new colour test missed it because it renders at 200x200, where the transposition is the identity. `NonSquareAreas()` now gives rMQR the same three entry points as the other two symbologies, at the same two sizes, which makes the arm reachable and kills the transposition (two failures) with four added cases. The rest is recorded as F9 instead of being pursued in a change about colours. The same round caught two more. `Render_TransparentColors_AreDrawnAsGiven` rendered onto a transparent ground, where "painted with `SrcOver`" and "erased" look the same, so a `SKBlendMode.Src` on the background paint passed every case in the class. It fails now that the ground is red, which matters because the previous commit removed such an erase path from the finder pass. And the builder remarks this round had just added repeated the previous round's error: they said a gradient wins "whatever the order of the two calls" without the `GradientDirection.None` exception that the same round had written into the renderer's docs and the migration guide.

The argument recorded against option C held for one overload of three. This plan and [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md) both said a colourless overload would let the old `Render(canvas, area, data, null, null)` compile silently. Three verifiers compiled both overload shapes: true on Standard QR, CS1503 on Micro QR and rMQR, which have no `IconData?` and would need the second `null` to reach `float moduleSizePercent`. Both documents are now qualified. The decision stands, and both already said it rested on other grounds, but the sentence claimed more than its measurement supported.

The one defect in the change itself was a generated file it did not regenerate. The committed Playground API page, `src/FeatherQR.Playground/wwwroot/api/index.html`, still published `SKColor? codeColor, SKColor? backgroundColor`. It is regenerated by hand on every public API change, as each of the four preceding commits did, and nothing gates it, because CI checks only `PublicAPI.approved.txt` and the release job rebuilds the HTML without comparing it. The change shipped a public page contradicting the assembly beside it, unnoticed because the file's own tooling described it as gitignored, which it is not. `tools/public_api.cs` now describes it correctly.
