A 26-round adversarial review of the branch then fixed the defects users would have hit (an interior U+FEFF that threw or was lost on decode, a text `Create` holds split in two, a parity that differed from the bytes written under a forced ISO-8859-1, advice that sent the caller to a second refusal) and moved the U+FEFF rule into the shared segmentation program for all three symbologies. The plan was folded on 2026-09-29:

- the design, decisions and lessons are in [standardqr-encoder.md](../specs/standardqr-encoder.md#structured-append), [standardqr-decoder.md](../specs/standardqr-decoder.md#decisions) and [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md)
- the corpus, the gate and the interop check are in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](../specs/qrcode-test-fixtures.md)
- the open items are F20 to F23 above.

Lessons. The specs keep these:

- a corpus that cannot fail is not a gate (odd repetitions, an odd number of accented characters), and the gate caught an oracle writing parity 0
- a rule held by one conditional needs a test that fails without it
- a fast path needs its definition beside it
- count when timing stops resolving
- a check after a search that did not know the rule is a second search
- a fix of a review finding is new code.

One belongs to this plan: the version cap the caller already had served as the count parameter, which kept the whole feature one method.

Benchmark delta: the single-symbol encode gained one predictable branch per data writer. `SimpleEncode` stayed within the machine's spread and allocations were identical. The decode path gained one `switch` case taken only on mode `0011`. The per-round numbers are in the encoder record.

### Phase 6, Kanji encoding (2026-09-29 to 2026-10-02)

Done. All three generators write ISO/IEC 18004 Kanji mode on request, through `AllowKanji`, off by default, on `QRCodeGeneratorOptions`, `MicroQRCodeGeneratorOptions` and `RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions`.
- A text qualifies when the charset is the library's choice (`EciMode.Default`, and on Standard QR no byte order mark) and every character is ASCII or has an encoder cell, which is JIS X 0208 without the seven cells CP932 reads differently.
- How it is written:
  - A text of cells alone is one Kanji segment with no ECI header, under both segmentations.
  - A text with ASCII in it is UTF-8 under `Single`. Under `Optimal` it is Kanji runs beside runs of its ASCII, where that plan is smaller than the UTF-8 plan.
  - Structured Append sets follow the same rule. Their parity is the XOR of the text's Shift_JIS bytes: 176 for the CodeGlyphX text, whose UTF-8 set carries 6.
- What was built:
  - The reverse table, generated from the sweep alongside the forward table and gated as its exact inverse (15,146 bytes).
  - The writers, and the capacity at every count width of each symbology.
  - An eighth segmentation state, with its own program and re-derived bounds in the three planners.
  - The Structured Append cost model and parity.
- Interop:
  - ZXing.Net reads every encoder cell in CI. zxing-cpp, ZXing.Net and CodeGlyphX read every cell in all three symbologies through `spot-check-kanji`.
  - Committed fixtures cover every Kanji count width, and an oracle test holds this library's symbols to them module for module.
- The default changed twice. From the single-mode flip on, Kanji mode was written unasked. It went back to UTF-8, with Kanji mode on request, after an Android 17 phone's own scanners read no Kanji-mode symbol. This was decided with the user on 2026-10-01.
- Not taken:
  - Kanji beside an ECI header: zxing-cpp reads such a segment in the ECI's charset, as the standard does.
  - Kanji in the Structured Append lanes, which stay seven-state.
- Speed: after the speed work a Kanji plan is still slower than its UTF-8 twin, by about 5-10 % on Standard QR and by more on Micro QR and rMQR. That was accepted, because the option is the caller's choice.
- Tag: `2.0.0-preview.4`.

The plan was folded on 2026-10-02:
- the rules and decisions into [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md#when-kanji-mode-is-written): "When Kanji mode is written", the reverse table and the scope row
- into the encoder records: [standardqr-encoder.md](../specs/standardqr-encoder.md) (segmentation, Structured Append, speed and lessons) and [rmqr-encoder.md](../specs/rmqr-encoder.md) (the Kanji scan)
- the fixtures, spot checks and oracle lessons into [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](../specs/qrcode-test-fixtures.md)
- the option into `docs/migration.md` and the README, and the capacities into the Kanji columns of `docs/data-capacity.md`.

Lessons. The specs keep these:
- an output default is judged by the readers people carry, and the phone scan belongs before the change
- an option has to reach every path that analyses the text
- a byte-for-byte comparison through the public API catches what the tests do not
- a hand edit to a generated file belongs in the generator
- a rule read literally can grow a symbol
- a comparison is benchmarked where it loses too
- a published table is a second reading
- a reader check confirms what it reads
- what a reuse saves depends on which filter accepts
- a harness warms past tiered compilation, and a shared machine is checked before it is timed.

One belongs to this plan: the bar "no slower than forced UTF-8" was set while Kanji mode was the default. Once Kanji mode became an option, meeting that bar was no longer required, and the cost became a trade the caller makes.

Benchmark delta:
- Without a Kanji plan: at every phase, text without a Kanji plan was compared byte for byte with the previous commit (52,716 cases), and its arms stayed within the machine's spread.
- With the option:
  - A text of cells alone encodes faster than its UTF-8 twin, with fewer bits and a smaller symbol.
  - A Kanji Structured Append set of 1,000 cells at versions up to 10-L is 33 % faster than the UTF-8 set (7 symbols against 12).
  - A Kanji plan on interleaved text is 5-35 % slower than its UTF-8 twin, which was accepted.
- Trimmed size: a trimmed consumer that only encodes QR pays about 22.5 KB for Kanji encoding, 115,200 → 138,240 bytes, recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

### Phase 6b, 128-bit tiers (2026-09-28 to 2026-10-01)

Done. Every scalar cell in the x64-without-AVX and WebAssembly columns of `SimdTiers.Expected` was raised or kept with its measured reason beside its row: the Structured Append parity and scanner stay scalar on x64, the rMQR value writers on ARM64, and six kernels on WebAssembly. 22 cells gained a portable 128-bit tier (9 of 11 on x64 without AVX, 13 of 19 on WebAssembly), as did the CPU-decided side of three more (the syndromes without GFNI, the rMQR extraction without fast PEXT, the luminance on ARM64 without the dot product), with `PackedSimd` steps where WebAssembly's own instruction won. The four existing tiers that lost to scalar on a default NativeAOT publish and on WebAssembly AOT were fixed first. Both report projects gained `--time` and `--parity`, and a parity test enters each tier directly. The confirming run found the WebAssembly text analysis slower than scalar when interpreted below 32 chars, so its threshold moved there from 8, and `--parity` got the tier's own entry. The public API is unchanged and no allocation was added. Its plan was folded into [the 128-bit round](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md#the-128-bit-round) and the per-symbology records, then deleted.

Lessons. The specs keep these:

- portable vector code in a default NativeAOT publish is limited to SSE2
- WebAssembly's runtimes disagree on a cast
- Mono's WebAssembly AOT turns some portable operations into calls into corlib
- the interpreter charges per operation and per call, its break-even point is higher than AOT's, and a fixed cost per decode hides there behind a share
- a dispatch change reaches callers whose cell did not change
- `--parity` through a dispatch only checks the tier the CI machine picks
- a share has to come from timing a stage alone.

Benchmark delta: end to end against main at the merge base, as the branch's time over main's, on default NativeAOT for win-x64 and linux-x64 and on WebAssembly AOT and interpreted: matrix decode 0.20 to 0.96, image decode 0.17 to 0.96, bitmap decode 0.20 to 0.47, the data-object API 0.25 to 1.01, encode 0.50 to 1.03, with the cells past 1.00 inside their runs' spread. Per-build figures are in [the 128-bit round](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md#the-128-bit-round). ARM64 (Apple M2) gave 0.87 to 1.02 with the dot product, and 0.57 to 0.69 for the bitmap decodes without it. Re-measured on 2026-10-02 against main 1cf1436, after the Kanji encoding and the shared decode pipeline: matrix decode 0.20 to 0.96, image decode 0.17 to 0.96, bitmap decode 0.20 to 0.48, the data-object API 0.23 to 1.02, encode 0.49 to 1.01, two new Kanji encodes 0.96 to 1.00. The three cells past 1.00 are small win-x64 encodes whose code is main's or shorter, so the cause is code placement. The spec's table is this measurement.

### Standard QR checks its ECC level and quiet zone up front (2026-10-02)

Done (F21, F22). Every Standard QR entry point (`Create`, the span `Create`, `CreateStructuredAppend`, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`) checks the ECC level and the quiet zone before it reads the content. Bounds, exception type, parameter names and order are Micro QR's and rMQR's: quiet zone (0 to 10,000), segmentation, level, then the fit. Both `QRCodeData` constructors take the same quiet-zone bound. `CalculateMatrixSize` lost its overflow check, which the bound makes unreachable.
- Tests: each argument through each of ten entry routes (plain, narrowed range, boost, `Optimal`, `Optimal` with a byte order mark, both span outputs, both sizings, Structured Append), past the bound on both sides and at it, plus the order across all three symbologies.
- Planted faults: each of the seven level checks removed, the level and quiet-zone bounds moved one step either way or dropped, the level compared signed, each constructor's check removed. 18 of 18 caught.
- The test that pinned Standard QR's `ArgumentException` as a frozen disagreement now pins the agreement.
- `OneSymbolText_DoesNotAnswerForTheSizeOfItsQuietZone` used a 30,000-module quiet zone that sizing refused and `Create` took. No such quiet zone exists now, so it checks the largest one instead.
- Found while fixing: `CreateStructuredAppend` overflowed `Size` as `Create` did, and the `QRCodeData` constructors took any quiet zone, negative included. Both are fixed here. An undefined `EciMode` and an undefined `QRCodeData` version are F24.

Lessons. The spec keeps one: an argument checked where it is first used is checked only on the routes that use it. One belongs to this plan: a test's premise can be the defect it works around. The one-symbol test needed sizing and `Create` to disagree on the quiet zone, which is what F22 removed.

Benchmark delta: `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd`, Release, in-process, 20 iterations, two branch and main runs interleaved. Numeric V1-L 887 and 790 ns against 926 and 833, Alphanumeric V1-M 850 and 850 against 859 and 848, Byte V40-L 78.3 and 76.8 µs against 74.8 and 76.5. Allocations identical (120 B, 3,985 B). The V40 pairs differ by +4.7 % and +0.4 %, and the ShortRun job in the same runs went the other way, so the change is inside the machine's spread.
